You are a web search agent. Follow your search method.

## Search method v000

Search the web for items that answer the hunt. Run searches, read results, and submit every item you find with a URL that supports it.

### Routing policy
Default route: Telem auto-routing (accuracy), tier default, 8 results per provider.
check_candidates route: same as default.
Use the default route for every search.

### Fetch policy
Fetch a page only when the search summaries are not enough.

You have $0.08 of Telem search budget. Every tool result reports what is left. When the budget runs out or you are done, call submit. Only submit items you have evidence for. Each find must cite a URL retrieved during this search whose text names the item; otherwise it scores as wrong.

<addendum>
## SiftText

SiftText is persistent memory across chats.

Entry: /Users/jack/sifttext/nodes/5e565245-14fe-406c-977c-cf94a9be246b/node.md
Retrieval guide: /Users/jack/sifttext/nodes/526ed0f5-4e5d-42b3-9e3f-b7ad429f2df8/node.md

At the start of every new chat, unless I say not to use SiftText, before any other tool call:
1. Run `sifttext instructions`.
2. Read the Entry above and follow it, plus any `agent-instructions` the command returns.
3. Before retrieving knowledge, read the Retrieval guide above, do not search first.

## Tooling policy

- Never directly invoke `python`, `python3`, `pip`, or `pip3` unless explicitly instructed by the human.
- Use `uv` for all agent-initiated Python work:
  - Python execution: `uv run python ...`
  - Scripts and tests: `uv run ...`
  - Throwaway dependencies: `uv run --with <package> ...`
  - Python CLI tools: `uvx <tool>`
  - Durable project dependencies: use the project's appropriate `uv` command and preserve its lockfile.
- For non-Python probing or testing with unavailable tools:
  - One executable: `nix run nixpkgs#<package> -- <args>`
  - Temporary environment: `nix shell nixpkgs#<package> ... --command <command>`
- Nix environments are temporary, but downloaded store paths may remain cached until garbage collection.
- If a Nix dependency becomes useful for recurring or future work, tell the human and suggest adding it to the appropriate durable Nix configuration (such as a project flake/dev shell, Home Manager, or nix-darwin configuration). Do not make that durable change unless asked.

</addendum>

## Contents

# REPORT ON LUNAR NOMENCLATURE

**by THE WORKING GROUP OF COMMISSION 17 OF THE IAU**  
   
 D. H. MENZEL, Chairman

M. MINNAERT\*

B. LEVIN

A. DOLLFUS (ex officio, as President of Commission 17)

B. BELL, Secretary

## 1. Introduction

At the Prague meeting of the IAU in [1967](/wiki/IAU_Transactions_XIIIB "IAU Transactions XIIIB"), a Working Group on Lunar Nomenclature was appointed, charged with the major responsibility of assigning names to craters on the Moon's far side. The members were Professor M. Minnaert, Professor A. Mikhailov, and Professor D. H. Menzel as Chairman; Professor A. Dollfus, as President of Commission 17, was a member ex officio. Later Professor B. Levin replaced Professor Mikhailov.  
   
 The Working Group held five formal meetings, the first in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and in New York City; the second in Paris, the third in Moscow, and the last two in Paris. In addition the four members have exchanged great quantities of correspondence. The list of 513 names presented herewith is a result of their study.  
   
 In order to obtain a list as completely representative and international as possible, the Chairmen made contact, through the National Academy of Sciences of the United States, with the national academies or equivalent organizations in other countries throughout the world. The great majority of these responded, giving information about potential nominees for crater names. All members of Commission 17 and members of the Executive Committee of the IAU were also contacted. We could not of course use all of the many suggestions we received. In addition, we incorporated a large number of the names from the list proposed by the U.S.S.R. Academy of Sciences after the observations of Zond 3.  
   
 To minimize the danger of confusion in oral usage, we eliminated one of any pair of names that sounded too similar, as well as names that resembled too closely others already assigned on the near side of the Moon. This procedure necessarily led to the exclusion of a number of highly distinguished names. For example, [Rutherford](/wiki/Rutherford "Rutherford") had to be omitted because of the crater [Rutherfurd](/wiki/Rutherfurd "Rutherfurd") on the near side, and [Born](/wiki/Born "Born") was excluded because of possible confusion with [Bohr](/wiki/Bohr "Bohr"). Some problems of this type remain in the earlier lists of [Blagg and Muller](/wiki/Named_Lunar_Formations "Named Lunar Formations") and of [Arthur](/index.php?title=IAU_Nomenclature&action=edit&redlink=1 "IAU Nomenclature (page does not exist)"), and need further study and clarification.  
   
 We divided the names into five categories according to relative distinction, so that we could assign the larger craters to persons of higher distinction.  
   
 The Working Group originally planned to assign the names in approximately alphabetical order, in latitude zones from the north to the south pole. This procedure would have made it practical to locate many of the craters on the maps without use of an index. Unavoidable exceptions to the rule occurred, however, and several cartographers objected on aesthetic grounds. The Working Group, after reconsideration, finally acceded to the preferences of the cartographers, and assigned names to craters, within each category of distinction, by the use of random numbers.  
   
 In so far as possible, the Working Group tried to assign names in such a way as to agree with the designations previously made by Professor Lipsky. However, we found that many of the craters named in his list, though well-defined, were considerably smaller than the limit we had arbitrarily set from the NASA Orbiter photographs. We had, therefore, to make some adjustments.  
   
 Also, certain previously named features, especially those on or near Mare Orientale, proved to be non-existent. As a result the names of five supposed mountain chains (Montes) must be cancelled: D'Alembert, Leibnitz, Doerfel, Hercynii, and Sovietici. We reassigned the name of D'Alembert to one of the larger craters. We also changed the names of three small features in the vicinity of [Mare Orientale](/wiki/Mare_Orientale "Mare Orientale") from Mare to Lacus: [Aestatis](/wiki/Lacus_Aestatis "Lacus Aestatis"), [Autumni](/wiki/Lacus_Autumni "Lacus Autumni"), and [Veris](/wiki/Lacus_Veris "Lacus Veris"). Rima Planck and Rima Schrödinger have been changed to [Vallis Planck](/wiki/Vallis_Planck "Vallis Planck") and [Vallis Schrödinger](/wiki/Vallis_Schr%C3%B6dinger "Vallis Schrödinger"). The formation Bouvard has been designated [Vallis Bouvard](/wiki/Vallis_Bouvard "Vallis Bouvard").  
   
 One of the larger features on the far side was given the name [Apollo](/wiki/Apollo "Apollo") to commemorate the USA program of that name for landing a man on the Moon. Like [Mare Moscoviense](/wiki/Mare_Moscoviense "Mare Moscoviense"), Apollo has many smaller craters in its vicinity which can be used for commemorative purposes. The names of deceased Soviet cosmonauts were assigned to features near [Mare Moscoviense](/wiki/Mare_Moscoviense "Mare Moscoviense"), and those of deceased American astronauts to features in the vicinity of Apollo, with one notable exception. The name of [Gagarin](/wiki/Gagarin "Gagarin"), the first man to orbit the Earth, was attached to one of the more prominent features on the far side.  
   
 The members of Commission 17 were invited to express their opinions on the question of using the names of living astronauts. Of those who replied, nearly all favored the use of the names of the men who participated in the first lunar landing, and a majority urged recognition of all of the Apollo astronauts who had either landed on or been in the vicinity of the Moon. The Working Group finally agreed to recognize the three astronauts of Apollo 8, who were the first to orbit the Moon and to see and photograph its far side, and the three astronauts of Apollo 11, who participated in the first landing of man on the Moon. The three astronauts of Apollo 8 were assigned craters in the vicinity of the crater Apollo, and those of Apollo 11 were assigned three previously un-named small craters near the landing point on [Mare Tranquillitatis](/wiki/Mare_Tranquillitatis "Mare Tranquillitatis"). In addition, the Working Group agreed that six distinguished living cosmonauts of the U.S.S.R. be accorded similar recognition by craters in the vicinity of [Mare Moscoviense](/wiki/Mare_Moscoviense "Mare Moscoviense").  
   
 The name Curie presented a special problem, which we finally resolved as follows, to avoid as far as possible duplication of names. The crater previously designated Joliot-Curie will henceforth be called [Joliot](/wiki/Joliot "Joliot"). At the request of the Polish members of Commission 17, we assigned a separate crater to Marie Curie, to be known as [Sklodowska](/wiki/Sklodowska "Sklodowska"), her maiden name. Finally, we named a third feature for Pierre Curie, to be known henceforth as [Curie](/wiki/Curie "Curie").  
   
 A number of years ago the British selenologist, [Wilkins](/wiki/Wilkins "Wilkins"), named the crater previously identified as Clavius B, on the near side, for Russell [Porter](/wiki/Porter "Porter"), the distinguished American amateur who had contributed in many ways to the development of astronomical science. He is perhaps best known for his beautiful drawings showing the detailed construction of the 200-in. Hale telescope. Although this name appeared on some lunar maps, it has never been formally accepted by the IAU. Since Porter was on our list anyway, we decided to assign his name officially to Clavius B. We propose to commemorate the 17 additional persons listed on p. 175 by adding them to features on the Moon already bearing their names.

On the afternoon of 20 August 1970 Professor Menzel presented the above material to the members of Commission 17 of the IAU as the Draft Report of the Working Group on Lunar Nomenclature. Several members of the Executive Committee of the IAU, including the President, Professor O. Heckmann, and the Secretary, Professor L. Perek, attended the meeting to evaluate the impact of the report on the Commission, especially the recommended inclusion of twelve living astronauts and cosmonauts.  
   
 The report was accepted with a few minor modifications by Commission 17 and by the General Assembly of the IAU, and the names and positions given herein are now official and authorized for use.  
   
 Commission 17 raised no objection to naming craters for six living USA astronauts and six living USSR cosmonauts. Also accepted was the proposal for naming a crater APOLLO, on the far side, to commemorate the USA Manned Landing Program and all who contributed to its success. It was further agreed that the actual landing spot of Apollo 11 should be officially named [Tranquility Base (Statio Tranquillitatis)](/wiki/Apollo_11_Site "Apollo 11 Site"), and that its location be marked with a small x on future maps, and that locations of [Sinus Lunicus](/wiki/Sinus_Lunicus "Sinus Lunicus") and [Planitia Descensus](/wiki/Planitia_Descensus "Planitia Descensus") be similarly marked.  
   
 At the meeting of Commission 17, D. W. G. Arthur raised objections to a few of the assignments on the grounds that the Working Group had departed from tradition by giving names to certain craters that lay within other very large craters, and that this practice would cause confusion later when Latin letter names were assigned to subordinate craters. It was agreed that the following names would be relocated: [Chappell](/wiki/Chappell "Chappell"), [Hagen](/wiki/Hagen "Hagen"), [Ingalls](/wiki/Ingalls "Ingalls"), [Krylov](/wiki/Krylov "Krylov"), and [Das](/wiki/Das "Das"). The new locations are given with the biographies.  
   
 Other objections were raised by Arthur and E. Whitaker to the proposed relocation of a few names from their [1964](/wiki/IAU_Transactions_XIIB "IAU Transactions XIIB") list, where the Working Group had been unable to find any feature in the original position on the ACIC maps. Subsequent to the IAU meeting and after the [official ACIC maps](/wiki/LMP "LMP") had been printed (Oct. 1970), Whitaker provided the Chairman of the Working Group with photographs of the original features thus establishing their existence, and it was determined that the names should be restored to their 1964 locations. These names were [Banachiewicz](/wiki/Banachiewicz "Banachiewicz"), [Boltzmann](/wiki/Boltzmann "Boltzmann"), [Hedin](/wiki/Hedin "Hedin"), [Lamarck](/wiki/Lamarck "Lamarck"), [Rayleigh](/wiki/Rayleigh "Rayleigh"), and [Riemann](/wiki/Riemann "Riemann"). Having reinstated [Riemann](/wiki/Riemann "Riemann"), we found it advisable to move [Rynin](/wiki/Rynin "Rynin") from its initial nearby position because of the similarity in pronounciation. The names of [Mandel'shtam](/wiki/Mandel%27shtam "Mandel'shtam") and [Butlerov](/wiki/Butlerov "Butlerov") were also shifted to new positions, as listed in the table.  
   
 This relocation left vacant a number of excellent far-side craters, To one of these, initially assigned to [Rayleigh](/wiki/Rayleigh "Rayleigh"), at 67S, 179E, we have provisionally assigned the name of [Minnaert](/wiki/Minnaert "Minnaert"), to honor the distinguished Dutch astronomer and astrophysicist who had participated so actively in our work on lunar nomenclature prior to his death in October 1970.  
   
 The report includes identifying notes on the names adopted by the IAU in [1964](/wiki/IAU_Transactions_XIIB "IAU Transactions XIIB") (Arthur's list) and in [1961](/wiki/IAU_Transactions_XIB "IAU Transactions XIB") (USSR list), as these data have not been previously available.  
   
 Mr. Robert W. Carder of the [Aeronautical Chart and Information Center](/wiki/DMA "DMA") (of the U.S. Air Force) gave invaluable assistance to the Working Group, providing us first with provisional lunar maps and later with the revised maps and printed overlays, which we used to make the assignments. He also supervised preparations of the Moon maps.

**Curie** is a large, degraded [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that lies along western rim and extends into the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_(Moon) "Far side (Moon)") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon").[[3]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-3) Hence, as seen from the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"), it can only be viewed from the side, with visibility depending on the effects of [libration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libration "Libration"). Curie crosses the northern edge of the proposed Australe megabasin. Nearby craters of note include [Schorr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schorr_(crater) "Schorr (crater)") to the northwest and the [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain "Walled plain") called [Sklodowska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sklodowska_(lunar_crater) "Sklodowska (lunar crater)") to the northeast. Attached to the southeastern rim is the heavily damaged walled plain [Lauritsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauritsen_(crater) "Lauritsen (crater)"). Both Sklodowska and Lauritsen are smaller than Curie.[[3]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-3)

This crater is named after French physicist and chemist [Pierre Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Curie "Pierre Curie") (1859–1906).[[4]](#cite_note-Menzel_et_al_1971-4) Its designation was formally adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1970.[[1]](#cite_note-GPN-1)

## Observations

This formation dates to the [Pre-Nectarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Nectarian "Pre-Nectarian") period of the [lunar geologic timescale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_geologic_timescale "Lunar geologic timescale").[[2]](#cite_note-Wilhelms_et_al_1987-2) The outer rim of Curie has been damaged and reshaped by nearby impacts. The sides of the rim are relatively linear, giving the crater an overall box-like shape. The eastern part of the rim is partly overlaid by the notable satellite craters Curie C to the northeast and Curie G along the east. At the northern end the rim is overlaid by the small crater Curie Z. Several other small craters lie along the rim, especially to the southwest.[[5]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-5): 99–100

The interior floor of Curie forms a relatively level plain, at least in comparison to the terrain that surrounds the crater. However this floor is disrupted in several locations by small impacts. A cluster of such impacts lies near the southwestern rim, with several of these craters overlapping each other. The small crater Curie K is located in the southeastern part of the floor, and Curie V lies alongside the northwestern inner wall.[[5]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-5): 99–100

# REPORT ON LUNAR NOMENCLATURE

**by THE WORKING GROUP OF COMMISSION 17 OF THE IAU**  
   
 D. H. MENZEL, Chairman

M. MINNAERT\*

B. LEVIN

A. DOLLFUS (ex officio, as President of Commission 17)

B. BELL, Secretary

## 1. Introduction

At the Prague meeting of the IAU in [1967](/wiki/IAU_Transactions_XIIIB "IAU Transactions XIIIB"), a Working Group on Lunar Nomenclature was appointed, charged with the major responsibility of assigning names to craters on the Moon's far side. The members were Professor M. Minnaert, Professor A. Mikhailov, and Professor D. H. Menzel as Chairman; Professor A. Dollfus, as President of Commission 17, was a member ex officio. Later Professor B. Levin replaced Professor Mikhailov.  
   
 The Working Group held five formal meetings, the first in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and in New York City; the second in Paris, the third in Moscow, and the last two in Paris. In addition the four members have exchanged great quantities of correspondence. The list of 513 names presented herewith is a result of their study.  
   
 In order to obtain a list as completely representative and international as possible, the Chairmen made contact, through the National Academy of Sciences of the United States, with the national academies or equivalent organizations in other countries throughout the world. The great majority of these responded, giving information about potential nominees for crater names. All members of Commission 17 and members of the Executive Committee of the IAU were also contacted. We could not of course use all of the many suggestions we received. In addition, we incorporated a large number of the names from the list proposed by the U.S.S.R. Academy of Sciences after the observations of Zond 3.  
   
 To minimize the danger of confusion in oral usage, we eliminated one of any pair of names that sounded too similar, as well as names that resembled too closely others already assigned on the near side of the Moon. This procedure necessarily led to the exclusion of a number of highly distinguished names. For example, [Rutherford](/wiki/Rutherford "Rutherford") had to be omitted because of the crater [Rutherfurd](/wiki/Rutherfurd "Rutherfurd") on the near side, and [Born](/wiki/Born "Born") was excluded because of possible confusion with [Bohr](/wiki/Bohr "Bohr"). Some problems of this type remain in the earlier lists of [Blagg and Muller](/wiki/Named_Lunar_Formations "Named Lunar Formations") and of [Arthur](/index.php?title=IAU_Nomenclature&action=edit&redlink=1 "IAU Nomenclature (page does not exist)"), and need further study and clarification.  
   
 We divided the names into five categories according to relative distinction, so that we could assign the larger craters to persons of higher distinction.  
   
 The Working Group originally planned to assign the names in approximately alphabetical order, in latitude zones from the north to the south pole. This procedure would have made it practical to locate many of the craters on the maps without use of an index. Unavoidable exceptions to the rule occurred, however, and several cartographers objected on aesthetic grounds. The Working Group, after reconsideration, finally acceded to the preferences of the cartographers, and assigned names to craters, within each category of distinction, by the use of random numbers.  
   
 In so far as possible, the Working Group tried to assign names in such a way as to agree with the designations previously made by Professor Lipsky. However, we found that many of the craters named in his list, though well-defined, were considerably smaller than the limit we had arbitrarily set from the NASA Orbiter photographs. We had, therefore, to make some adjustments.  
   
 Also, certain previously named features, especially those on or near Mare Orientale, proved to be non-existent. As a result the names of five supposed mountain chains (Montes) must be cancelled: D'Alembert, Leibnitz, Doerfel, Hercynii, and Sovietici. We reassigned the name of D'Alembert to one of the larger craters. We also changed the names of three small features in the vicinity of [Mare Orientale](/wiki/Mare_Orientale "Mare Orientale") from Mare to Lacus: [Aestatis](/wiki/Lacus_Aestatis "Lacus Aestatis"), [Autumni](/wiki/Lacus_Autumni "Lacus Autumni"), and [Veris](/wiki/Lacus_Veris "Lacus Veris"). Rima Planck and Rima Schrödinger have been changed to [Vallis Planck](/wiki/Vallis_Planck "Vallis Planck") and [Vallis Schrödinger](/wiki/Vallis_Schr%C3%B6dinger "Vallis Schrödinger"). The formation Bouvard has been designated [Vallis Bouvard](/wiki/Vallis_Bouvard "Vallis Bouvard").  
   
 One of the larger features on the far side was given the name [Apollo](/wiki/Apollo "Apollo") to commemorate the USA program of that name for landing a man on the Moon. Like [Mare Moscoviense](/wiki/Mare_Moscoviense "Mare Moscoviense"), Apollo has many smaller craters in its vicinity which can be used for commemorative purposes. The names of deceased Soviet cosmonauts were assigned to features near [Mare Moscoviense](/wiki/Mare_Moscoviense "Mare Moscoviense"), and those of deceased American astronauts to features in the vicinity of Apollo, with one notable exception. The name of [Gagarin](/wiki/Gagarin "Gagarin"), the first man to orbit the Earth, was attached to one of the more prominent features on the far side.  
   
 The members of Commission 17 were invited to express their opinions on the question of using the names of living astronauts. Of those who replied, nearly all favored the use of the names of the men who participated in the first lunar landing, and a majority urged recognition of all of the Apollo astronauts who had either landed on or been in the vicinity of the Moon. The Working Group finally agreed to recognize the three astronauts of Apollo 8, who were the first to orbit the Moon and to see and photograph its far side, and the three astronauts of Apollo 11, who participated in the first landing of man on the Moon. The three astronauts of Apollo 8 were assigned craters in the vicinity of the crater Apollo, and those of Apollo 11 were assigned three previously un-named small craters near the landing point on [Mare Tranquillitatis](/wiki/Mare_Tranquillitatis "Mare Tranquillitatis"). In addition, the Working Group agreed that six distinguished living cosmonauts of the U.S.S.R. be accorded similar recognition by craters in the vicinity of [Mare Moscoviense](/wiki/Mare_Moscoviense "Mare Moscoviense").  
   
 The name Curie presented a special problem, which we finally resolved as follows, to avoid as far as possible duplication of names. The crater previously designated Joliot-Curie will henceforth be called [Joliot](/wiki/Joliot "Joliot"). At the request of the Polish members of Commission 17, we assigned a separate crater to Marie Curie, to be known as [Sklodowska](/wiki/Sklodowska "Sklodowska"), her maiden name. Finally, we named a third feature for Pierre Curie, to be known henceforth as [Curie](/wiki/Curie "Curie").  
   
 A number of years ago the British selenologist, [Wilkins](/wiki/Wilkins "Wilkins"), named the crater previously identified as Clavius B, on the near side, for Russell [Porter](/wiki/Porter "Porter"), the distinguished American amateur who had contributed in many ways to the development of astronomical science. He is perhaps best known for his beautiful drawings showing the detailed construction of the 200-in. Hale telescope. Although this name appeared on some lunar maps, it has never been formally accepted by the IAU. Since Porter was on our list anyway, we decided to assign his name officially to Clavius B. We propose to commemorate the 17 additional persons listed on p. 175 by adding them to features on the Moon already bearing their names.  
   
 The biographical notes on all the persons selected, which form the balance of this report, were prepared by Dr Barbara Bell, of the Harvard College Observatory, with the assistance of the members of the Working Group. The source of data on each name is identified as follows:

On the afternoon of 20 August 1970 Professor Menzel presented the above material to the members of Commission 17 of the IAU as the Draft Report of the Working Group on Lunar Nomenclature. Several members of the Executive Committee of the IAU, including the President, Professor O. Heckmann, and the Secretary, Professor L. Perek, attended the meeting to evaluate the impact of the report on the Commission, especially the recommended inclusion of twelve living astronauts and cosmonauts.  
   
 The report was accepted with a few minor modifications by Commission 17 and by the General Assembly of the IAU, and the names and positions given herein are now official and authorized for use.  
   
 Commission 17 raised no objection to naming craters for six living USA astronauts and six living USSR cosmonauts. Also accepted was the proposal for naming a crater APOLLO, on the far side, to commemorate the USA Manned Landing Program and all who contributed to its success. It was further agreed that the actual landing spot of Apollo 11 should be officially named [Tranquility Base (Statio Tranquillitatis)](/wiki/Apollo_11_Site "Apollo 11 Site"), and that its location be marked with a small x on future maps, and that locations of [Sinus Lunicus](/wiki/Sinus_Lunicus "Sinus Lunicus") and [Planitia Descensus](/wiki/Planitia_Descensus "Planitia Descensus") be similarly marked.  
   
 At the meeting of Commission 17, D. W. G. Arthur raised objections to a few of the assignments on the grounds that the Working Group had departed from tradition by giving names to certain craters that lay within other very large craters, and that this practice would cause confusion later when Latin letter names were assigned to subordinate craters. It was agreed that the following names would be relocated: [Chappell](/wiki/Chappell "Chappell"), [Hagen](/wiki/Hagen "Hagen"), [Ingalls](/wiki/Ingalls "Ingalls"), [Krylov](/wiki/Krylov "Krylov"), and [Das](/wiki/Das "Das"). The new locations are given with the biographies.  
   
 Other objections were raised by Arthur and E. Whitaker to the proposed relocation of a few names from their [1964](/wiki/IAU_Transactions_XIIB "IAU Transactions XIIB") list, where the Working Group had been unable to find any feature in the original position on the ACIC maps. Subsequent to the IAU meeting and after the [official ACIC maps](/wiki/LMP "LMP") had been printed (Oct. 1970), Whitaker provided the Chairman of the Working Group with photographs of the original features thus establishing their existence, and it was determined that the names should be restored to their 1964 locations. These names were [Banachiewicz](/wiki/Banachiewicz "Banachiewicz"), [Boltzmann](/wiki/Boltzmann "Boltzmann"), [Hedin](/wiki/Hedin "Hedin"), [Lamarck](/wiki/Lamarck "Lamarck"), [Rayleigh](/wiki/Rayleigh "Rayleigh"), and [Riemann](/wiki/Riemann "Riemann"). Having reinstated [Riemann](/wiki/Riemann "Riemann"), we found it advisable to move [Rynin](/wiki/Rynin "Rynin") from its initial nearby position because of the similarity in pronounciation. The names of [Mandel'shtam](/wiki/Mandel%27shtam "Mandel'shtam") and [Butlerov](/wiki/Butlerov "Butlerov") were also shifted to new positions, as listed in the table.

**Curie** is a large, degraded [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that lies along western rim and extends into the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_(Moon) "Far side (Moon)") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon").[[3]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-3) Hence, as seen from the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"), it can only be viewed from the side, with visibility depending on the effects of [libration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libration "Libration"). Curie crosses the northern edge of the proposed Australe megabasin. Nearby craters of note include [Schorr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schorr_(crater) "Schorr (crater)") to the northwest and the [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain "Walled plain") called [Sklodowska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sklodowska_(lunar_crater) "Sklodowska (lunar crater)") to the northeast. Attached to the southeastern rim is the heavily damaged walled plain [Lauritsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauritsen_(crater) "Lauritsen (crater)"). Both Sklodowska and Lauritsen are smaller than Curie.[[3]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-3)

This crater is named after French physicist and chemist [Pierre Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Curie "Pierre Curie") (1859–1906).[[4]](#cite_note-Menzel_et_al_1971-4) Its designation was formally adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1970.[[1]](#cite_note-GPN-1)

## Observations

This formation dates to the [Pre-Nectarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Nectarian "Pre-Nectarian") period of the [lunar geologic timescale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_geologic_timescale "Lunar geologic timescale").[[2]](#cite_note-Wilhelms_et_al_1987-2) The outer rim of Curie has been damaged and reshaped by nearby impacts. The sides of the rim are relatively linear, giving the crater an overall box-like shape. The eastern part of the rim is partly overlaid by the notable satellite craters Curie C to the northeast and Curie G along the east. At the northern end the rim is overlaid by the small crater Curie Z. Several other small craters lie along the rim, especially to the southwest.[[5]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-5): 99–100

The interior floor of Curie forms a relatively level plain, at least in comparison to the terrain that surrounds the crater. However this floor is disrupted in several locations by small impacts. A cluster of such impacts lies near the southwestern rim, with several of these craters overlapping each other. The small crater Curie K is located in the southeastern part of the floor, and Curie V lies alongside the northwestern inner wall.[[5]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-5): 99–100

# REPORT ON LUNAR NOMENCLATURE

**by THE WORKING GROUP OF COMMISSION 17 OF THE IAU**  
   
 D. H. MENZEL, Chairman

M. MINNAERT\*

B. LEVIN

A. DOLLFUS (ex officio, as President of Commission 17)

B. BELL, Secretary

## 1. Introduction

At the Prague meeting of the IAU in [1967](/wiki/IAU_Transactions_XIIIB "IAU Transactions XIIIB"), a Working Group on Lunar Nomenclature was appointed, charged with the major responsibility of assigning names to craters on the Moon's far side. The members were Professor M. Minnaert, Professor A. Mikhailov, and Professor D. H. Menzel as Chairman; Professor A. Dollfus, as President of Commission 17, was a member ex officio. Later Professor B. Levin replaced Professor Mikhailov.  
   
 The Working Group held five formal meetings, the first in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and in New York City; the second in Paris, the third in Moscow, and the last two in Paris. In addition the four members have exchanged great quantities of correspondence. The list of 513 names presented herewith is a result of their study.  
   
 In order to obtain a list as completely representative and international as possible, the Chairmen made contact, through the National Academy of Sciences of the United States, with the national academies or equivalent organizations in other countries throughout the world. The great majority of these responded, giving information about potential nominees for crater names. All members of Commission 17 and members of the Executive Committee of the IAU were also contacted. We could not of course use all of the many suggestions we received. In addition, we incorporated a large number of the names from the list proposed by the U.S.S.R. Academy of Sciences after the observations of Zond 3.  
   
 To minimize the danger of confusion in oral usage, we eliminated one of any pair of names that sounded too similar, as well as names that resembled too closely others already assigned on the near side of the Moon. This procedure necessarily led to the exclusion of a number of highly distinguished names. For example, [Rutherford](/wiki/Rutherford "Rutherford") had to be omitted because of the crater [Rutherfurd](/wiki/Rutherfurd "Rutherfurd") on the near side, and [Born](/wiki/Born "Born") was excluded because of possible confusion with [Bohr](/wiki/Bohr "Bohr"). Some problems of this type remain in the earlier lists of [Blagg and Muller](/wiki/Named_Lunar_Formations "Named Lunar Formations") and of [Arthur](/index.php?title=IAU_Nomenclature&action=edit&redlink=1 "IAU Nomenclature (page does not exist)"), and need further study and clarification.  
   
 We divided the names into five categories according to relative distinction, so that we could assign the larger craters to persons of higher distinction.  
   
 The Working Group originally planned to assign the names in approximately alphabetical order, in latitude zones from the north to the south pole. This procedure would have made it practical to locate many of the craters on the maps without use of an index. Unavoidable exceptions to the rule occurred, however, and several cartographers objected on aesthetic grounds. The Working Group, after reconsideration, finally acceded to the preferences of the cartographers, and assigned names to craters, within each category of distinction, by the use of random numbers.  
   
 In so far as possible, the Working Group tried to assign names in such a way as to agree with the designations previously made by Professor Lipsky. However, we found that many of the craters named in his list, though well-defined, were considerably smaller than the limit we had arbitrarily set from the NASA Orbiter photographs. We had, therefore, to make some adjustments.  
   
 Also, certain previously named features, especially those on or near Mare Orientale, proved to be non-existent. As a result the names of five supposed mountain chains (Montes) must be cancelled: D'Alembert, Leibnitz, Doerfel, Hercynii, and Sovietici. We reassigned the name of D'Alembert to one of the larger craters. We also changed the names of three small features in the vicinity of [Mare Orientale](/wiki/Mare_Orientale "Mare Orientale") from Mare to Lacus: [Aestatis](/wiki/Lacus_Aestatis "Lacus Aestatis"), [Autumni](/wiki/Lacus_Autumni "Lacus Autumni"), and [Veris](/wiki/Lacus_Veris "Lacus Veris"). Rima Planck and Rima Schrödinger have been changed to [Vallis Planck](/wiki/Vallis_Planck "Vallis Planck") and [Vallis Schrödinger](/wiki/Vallis_Schr%C3%B6dinger "Vallis Schrödinger"). The formation Bouvard has been designated [Vallis Bouvard](/wiki/Vallis_Bouvard "Vallis Bouvard").  
   
 One of the larger features on the far side was given the name [Apollo](/wiki/Apollo "Apollo") to commemorate the USA program of that name for landing a man on the Moon. Like [Mare Moscoviense](/wiki/Mare_Moscoviense "Mare Moscoviense"), Apollo has many smaller craters in its vicinity which can be used for commemorative purposes. The names of deceased Soviet cosmonauts were assigned to features near [Mare Moscoviense](/wiki/Mare_Moscoviense "Mare Moscoviense"), and those of deceased American astronauts to features in the vicinity of Apollo, with one notable exception. The name of [Gagarin](/wiki/Gagarin "Gagarin"), the first man to orbit the Earth, was attached to one of the more prominent features on the far side.  
   
 The members of Commission 17 were invited to express their opinions on the question of using the names of living astronauts. Of those who replied, nearly all favored the use of the names of the men who participated in the first lunar landing, and a majority urged recognition of all of the Apollo astronauts who had either landed on or been in the vicinity of the Moon. The Working Group finally agreed to recognize the three astronauts of Apollo 8, who were the first to orbit the Moon and to see and photograph its far side, and the three astronauts of Apollo 11, who participated in the first landing of man on the Moon. The three astronauts of Apollo 8 were assigned craters in the vicinity of the crater Apollo, and those of Apollo 11 were assigned three previously un-named small craters near the landing point on [Mare Tranquillitatis](/wiki/Mare_Tranquillitatis "Mare Tranquillitatis"). In addition, the Working Group agreed that six distinguished living cosmonauts of the U.S.S.R. be accorded similar recognition by craters in the vicinity of [Mare Moscoviense](/wiki/Mare_Moscoviense "Mare Moscoviense").  
   
 The name Curie presented a special problem, which we finally resolved as follows, to avoid as far as possible duplication of names. The crater previously designated Joliot-Curie will henceforth be called [Joliot](/wiki/Joliot "Joliot"). At the request of the Polish members of Commission 17, we assigned a separate crater to Marie Curie, to be known as [Sklodowska](/wiki/Sklodowska "Sklodowska"), her maiden name. Finally, we named a third feature for Pierre Curie, to be known henceforth as [Curie](/wiki/Curie "Curie").  
   
 A number of years ago the British selenologist, [Wilkins](/wiki/Wilkins "Wilkins"), named the crater previously identified as Clavius B, on the near side, for Russell [Porter](/wiki/Porter "Porter"), the distinguished American amateur who had contributed in many ways to the development of astronomical science. He is perhaps best known for his beautiful drawings showing the detailed construction of the 200-in. Hale telescope. Although this name appeared on some lunar maps, it has never been formally accepted by the IAU. Since Porter was on our list anyway, we decided to assign his name officially to Clavius B. We propose to commemorate the 17 additional persons listed on p. 175 by adding them to features on the Moon already bearing their names.

On the afternoon of 20 August 1970 Professor Menzel presented the above material to the members of Commission 17 of the IAU as the Draft Report of the Working Group on Lunar Nomenclature. Several members of the Executive Committee of the IAU, including the President, Professor O. Heckmann, and the Secretary, Professor L. Perek, attended the meeting to evaluate the impact of the report on the Commission, especially the recommended inclusion of twelve living astronauts and cosmonauts.  
   
 The report was accepted with a few minor modifications by Commission 17 and by the General Assembly of the IAU, and the names and positions given herein are now official and authorized for use.  
   
 Commission 17 raised no objection to naming craters for six living USA astronauts and six living USSR cosmonauts. Also accepted was the proposal for naming a crater APOLLO, on the far side, to commemorate the USA Manned Landing Program and all who contributed to its success. It was further agreed that the actual landing spot of Apollo 11 should be officially named [Tranquility Base (Statio Tranquillitatis)](/wiki/Apollo_11_Site "Apollo 11 Site"), and that its location be marked with a small x on future maps, and that locations of [Sinus Lunicus](/wiki/Sinus_Lunicus "Sinus Lunicus") and [Planitia Descensus](/wiki/Planitia_Descensus "Planitia Descensus") be similarly marked.  
   
 At the meeting of Commission 17, D. W. G. Arthur raised objections to a few of the assignments on the grounds that the Working Group had departed from tradition by giving names to certain craters that lay within other very large craters, and that this practice would cause confusion later when Latin letter names were assigned to subordinate craters. It was agreed that the following names would be relocated: [Chappell](/wiki/Chappell "Chappell"), [Hagen](/wiki/Hagen "Hagen"), [Ingalls](/wiki/Ingalls "Ingalls"), [Krylov](/wiki/Krylov "Krylov"), and [Das](/wiki/Das "Das"). The new locations are given with the biographies.  
   
 Other objections were raised by Arthur and E. Whitaker to the proposed relocation of a few names from their [1964](/wiki/IAU_Transactions_XIIB "IAU Transactions XIIB") list, where the Working Group had been unable to find any feature in the original position on the ACIC maps. Subsequent to the IAU meeting and after the [official ACIC maps](/wiki/LMP "LMP") had been printed (Oct. 1970), Whitaker provided the Chairman of the Working Group with photographs of the original features thus establishing their existence, and it was determined that the names should be restored to their 1964 locations. These names were [Banachiewicz](/wiki/Banachiewicz "Banachiewicz"), [Boltzmann](/wiki/Boltzmann "Boltzmann"), [Hedin](/wiki/Hedin "Hedin"), [Lamarck](/wiki/Lamarck "Lamarck"), [Rayleigh](/wiki/Rayleigh "Rayleigh"), and [Riemann](/wiki/Riemann "Riemann"). Having reinstated [Riemann](/wiki/Riemann "Riemann"), we found it advisable to move [Rynin](/wiki/Rynin "Rynin") from its initial nearby position because of the similarity in pronounciation. The names of [Mandel'shtam](/wiki/Mandel%27shtam "Mandel'shtam") and [Butlerov](/wiki/Butlerov "Butlerov") were also shifted to new positions, as listed in the table.  
   
 This relocation left vacant a number of excellent far-side craters, To one of these, initially assigned to [Rayleigh](/wiki/Rayleigh "Rayleigh"), at 67S, 179E, we have provisionally assigned the name of [Minnaert](/wiki/Minnaert "Minnaert"), to honor the distinguished Dutch astronomer and astrophysicist who had participated so actively in our work on lunar nomenclature prior to his death in October 1970.  
   
 The report includes identifying notes on the names adopted by the IAU in [1964](/wiki/IAU_Transactions_XIIB "IAU Transactions XIIB") (Arthur's list) and in [1961](/wiki/IAU_Transactions_XIB "IAU Transactions XIB") (USSR list), as these data have not been previously available.  
   
 Mr. Robert W. Carder of the [Aeronautical Chart and Information Center](/wiki/DMA "DMA") (of the U.S. Air Force) gave invaluable assistance to the Working Group, providing us first with provisional lunar maps and later with the revised maps and printed overlays, which we used to make the assignments. He also supervised preparations of the Moon maps.  
   
 Grant NGR 22-007-194 from NASA supported a portion of the work of Professor Menzel and the major part of the work of Dr Bell on this project.

**Curie** is a large, degraded [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that lies along western rim and extends into the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_(Moon) "Far side (Moon)") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon").[[3]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-3) Hence, as seen from the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"), it can only be viewed from the side, with visibility depending on the effects of [libration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libration "Libration"). Curie crosses the northern edge of the proposed Australe megabasin. Nearby craters of note include [Schorr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schorr_(crater) "Schorr (crater)") to the northwest and the [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain "Walled plain") called [Sklodowska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sklodowska_(lunar_crater) "Sklodowska (lunar crater)") to the northeast. Attached to the southeastern rim is the heavily damaged walled plain [Lauritsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauritsen_(crater) "Lauritsen (crater)"). Both Sklodowska and Lauritsen are smaller than Curie.[[3]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-3)

This crater is named after French physicist and chemist [Pierre Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Curie "Pierre Curie") (1859–1906).[[4]](#cite_note-Menzel_et_al_1971-4) Its designation was formally adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1970.[[1]](#cite_note-GPN-1)

## Observations

This formation dates to the [Pre-Nectarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Nectarian "Pre-Nectarian") period of the [lunar geologic timescale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_geologic_timescale "Lunar geologic timescale").[[2]](#cite_note-Wilhelms_et_al_1987-2) The outer rim of Curie has been damaged and reshaped by nearby impacts. The sides of the rim are relatively linear, giving the crater an overall box-like shape. The eastern part of the rim is partly overlaid by the notable satellite craters Curie C to the northeast and Curie G along the east. At the northern end the rim is overlaid by the small crater Curie Z. Several other small craters lie along the rim, especially to the southwest.[[5]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-5): 99–100

The interior floor of Curie forms a relatively level plain, at least in comparison to the terrain that surrounds the crater. However this floor is disrupted in several locations by small impacts. A cluster of such impacts lies near the southwestern rim, with several of these craters overlapping each other. The small crater Curie K is located in the southeastern part of the floor, and Curie V lies alongside the northwestern inner wall.[[5]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-5): 99–100

# REPORT ON LUNAR NOMENCLATURE

**by THE WORKING GROUP OF COMMISSION 17 OF THE IAU**  
   
 D. H. MENZEL, Chairman

M. MINNAERT\*

B. LEVIN

A. DOLLFUS (ex officio, as President of Commission 17)

B. BELL, Secretary

## 1. Introduction

At the Prague meeting of the IAU in [1967](/wiki/IAU_Transactions_XIIIB "IAU Transactions XIIIB"), a Working Group on Lunar Nomenclature was appointed, charged with the major responsibility of assigning names to craters on the Moon's far side. The members were Professor M. Minnaert, Professor A. Mikhailov, and Professor D. H. Menzel as Chairman; Professor A. Dollfus, as President of Commission 17, was a member ex officio. Later Professor B. Levin replaced Professor Mikhailov.  
   
 The Working Group held five formal meetings, the first in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and in New York City; the second in Paris, the third in Moscow, and the last two in Paris. In addition the four members have exchanged great quantities of correspondence. The list of 513 names presented herewith is a result of their study.  
   
 In order to obtain a list as completely representative and international as possible, the Chairmen made contact, through the National Academy of Sciences of the United States, with the national academies or equivalent organizations in other countries throughout the world. The great majority of these responded, giving information about potential nominees for crater names. All members of Commission 17 and members of the Executive Committee of the IAU were also contacted. We could not of course use all of the many suggestions we received. In addition, we incorporated a large number of the names from the list proposed by the U.S.S.R. Academy of Sciences after the observations of Zond 3.  
   
 To minimize the danger of confusion in oral usage, we eliminated one of any pair of names that sounded too similar, as well as names that resembled too closely others already assigned on the near side of the Moon. This procedure necessarily led to the exclusion of a number of highly distinguished names. For example, [Rutherford](/wiki/Rutherford "Rutherford") had to be omitted because of the crater [Rutherfurd](/wiki/Rutherfurd "Rutherfurd") on the near side, and [Born](/wiki/Born "Born") was excluded because of possible confusion with [Bohr](/wiki/Bohr "Bohr"). Some problems of this type remain in the earlier lists of [Blagg and Muller](/wiki/Named_Lunar_Formations "Named Lunar Formations") and of [Arthur](/index.php?title=IAU_Nomenclature&action=edit&redlink=1 "IAU Nomenclature (page does not exist)"), and need further study and clarification.  
   
 We divided the names into five categories according to relative distinction, so that we could assign the larger craters to persons of higher distinction.  
   
 The Working Group originally planned to assign the names in approximately alphabetical order, in latitude zones from the north to the south pole. This procedure would have made it practical to locate many of the craters on the maps without use of an index. Unavoidable exceptions to the rule occurred, however, and several cartographers objected on aesthetic grounds. The Working Group, after reconsideration, finally acceded to the preferences of the cartographers, and assigned names to craters, within each category of distinction, by the use of random numbers.  
   
 In so far as possible, the Working Group tried to assign names in such a way as to agree with the designations previously made by Professor Lipsky. However, we found that many of the craters named in his list, though well-defined, were considerably smaller than the limit we had arbitrarily set from the NASA Orbiter photographs. We had, therefore, to make some adjustments.  
   
 Also, certain previously named features, especially those on or near Mare Orientale, proved to be non-existent. As a result the names of five supposed mountain chains (Montes) must be cancelled: D'Alembert, Leibnitz, Doerfel, Hercynii, and Sovietici. We reassigned the name of D'Alembert to one of the larger craters. We also changed the names of three small features in the vicinity of [Mare Orientale](/wiki/Mare_Orientale "Mare Orientale") from Mare to Lacus: [Aestatis](/wiki/Lacus_Aestatis "Lacus Aestatis"), [Autumni](/wiki/Lacus_Autumni "Lacus Autumni"), and [Veris](/wiki/Lacus_Veris "Lacus Veris"). Rima Planck and Rima Schrödinger have been changed to [Vallis Planck](/wiki/Vallis_Planck "Vallis Planck") and [Vallis Schrödinger](/wiki/Vallis_Schr%C3%B6dinger "Vallis Schrödinger"). The formation Bouvard has been designated [Vallis Bouvard](/wiki/Vallis_Bouvard "Vallis Bouvard").  
   
 One of the larger features on the far side was given the name [Apollo](/wiki/Apollo "Apollo") to commemorate the USA program of that name for landing a man on the Moon. Like [Mare Moscoviense](/wiki/Mare_Moscoviense "Mare Moscoviense"), Apollo has many smaller craters in its vicinity which can be used for commemorative purposes. The names of deceased Soviet cosmonauts were assigned to features near [Mare Moscoviense](/wiki/Mare_Moscoviense "Mare Moscoviense"), and those of deceased American astronauts to features in the vicinity of Apollo, with one notable exception. The name of [Gagarin](/wiki/Gagarin "Gagarin"), the first man to orbit the Earth, was attached to one of the more prominent features on the far side.  
   
 The members of Commission 17 were invited to express their opinions on the question of using the names of living astronauts. Of those who replied, nearly all favored the use of the names of the men who participated in the first lunar landing, and a majority urged recognition of all of the Apollo astronauts who had either landed on or been in the vicinity of the Moon. The Working Group finally agreed to recognize the three astronauts of Apollo 8, who were the first to orbit the Moon and to see and photograph its far side, and the three astronauts of Apollo 11, who participated in the first landing of man on the Moon. The three astronauts of Apollo 8 were assigned craters in the vicinity of the crater Apollo, and those of Apollo 11 were assigned three previously un-named small craters near the landing point on [Mare Tranquillitatis](/wiki/Mare_Tranquillitatis "Mare Tranquillitatis"). In addition, the Working Group agreed that six distinguished living cosmonauts of the U.S.S.R. be accorded similar recognition by craters in the vicinity of [Mare Moscoviense](/wiki/Mare_Moscoviense "Mare Moscoviense").  
   
 The name Curie presented a special problem, which we finally resolved as follows, to avoid as far as possible duplication of names. The crater previously designated Joliot-Curie will henceforth be called [Joliot](/wiki/Joliot "Joliot"). At the request of the Polish members of Commission 17, we assigned a separate crater to Marie Curie, to be known as [Sklodowska](/wiki/Sklodowska "Sklodowska"), her maiden name. Finally, we named a third feature for Pierre Curie, to be known henceforth as [Curie](/wiki/Curie "Curie").  
   
 A number of years ago the British selenologist, [Wilkins](/wiki/Wilkins "Wilkins"), named the crater previously identified as Clavius B, on the near side, for Russell [Porter](/wiki/Porter "Porter"), the distinguished American amateur who had contributed in many ways to the development of astronomical science. He is perhaps best known for his beautiful drawings showing the detailed construction of the 200-in. Hale telescope. Although this name appeared on some lunar maps, it has never been formally accepted by the IAU. Since Porter was on our list anyway, we decided to assign his name officially to Clavius B. We propose to commemorate the 17 additional persons listed on p. 175 by adding them to features on the Moon already bearing their names.  
   
 The biographical notes on all the persons selected, which form the balance of this report, were prepared by Dr Barbara Bell, of the Harvard College Observatory, with the assistance of the members of the Working Group. The source of data on each name is identified as follows:

On the afternoon of 20 August 1970 Professor Menzel presented the above material to the members of Commission 17 of the IAU as the Draft Report of the Working Group on Lunar Nomenclature. Several members of the Executive Committee of the IAU, including the President, Professor O. Heckmann, and the Secretary, Professor L. Perek, attended the meeting to evaluate the impact of the report on the Commission, especially the recommended inclusion of twelve living astronauts and cosmonauts.  
   
 The report was accepted with a few minor modifications by Commission 17 and by the General Assembly of the IAU, and the names and positions given herein are now official and authorized for use.  
   
 Commission 17 raised no objection to naming craters for six living USA astronauts and six living USSR cosmonauts. Also accepted was the proposal for naming a crater APOLLO, on the far side, to commemorate the USA Manned Landing Program and all who contributed to its success. It was further agreed that the actual landing spot of Apollo 11 should be officially named [Tranquility Base (Statio Tranquillitatis)](/wiki/Apollo_11_Site "Apollo 11 Site"), and that its location be marked with a small x on future maps, and that locations of [Sinus Lunicus](/wiki/Sinus_Lunicus "Sinus Lunicus") and [Planitia Descensus](/wiki/Planitia_Descensus "Planitia Descensus") be similarly marked.  
   
 At the meeting of Commission 17, D. W. G. Arthur raised objections to a few of the assignments on the grounds that the Working Group had departed from tradition by giving names to certain craters that lay within other very large craters, and that this practice would cause confusion later when Latin letter names were assigned to subordinate craters. It was agreed that the following names would be relocated: [Chappell](/wiki/Chappell "Chappell"), [Hagen](/wiki/Hagen "Hagen"), [Ingalls](/wiki/Ingalls "Ingalls"), [Krylov](/wiki/Krylov "Krylov"), and [Das](/wiki/Das "Das"). The new locations are given with the biographies.  
   
 Other objections were raised by Arthur and E. Whitaker to the proposed relocation of a few names from their [1964](/wiki/IAU_Transactions_XIIB "IAU Transactions XIIB") list, where the Working Group had been unable to find any feature in the original position on the ACIC maps. Subsequent to the IAU meeting and after the [official ACIC maps](/wiki/LMP "LMP") had been printed (Oct. 1970), Whitaker provided the Chairman of the Working Group with photographs of the original features thus establishing their existence, and it was determined that the names should be restored to their 1964 locations. These names were [Banachiewicz](/wiki/Banachiewicz "Banachiewicz"), [Boltzmann](/wiki/Boltzmann "Boltzmann"), [Hedin](/wiki/Hedin "Hedin"), [Lamarck](/wiki/Lamarck "Lamarck"), [Rayleigh](/wiki/Rayleigh "Rayleigh"), and [Riemann](/wiki/Riemann "Riemann"). Having reinstated [Riemann](/wiki/Riemann "Riemann"), we found it advisable to move [Rynin](/wiki/Rynin "Rynin") from its initial nearby position because of the similarity in pronounciation. The names of [Mandel'shtam](/wiki/Mandel%27shtam "Mandel'shtam") and [Butlerov](/wiki/Butlerov "Butlerov") were also shifted to new positions, as listed in the table.  
   
 This relocation left vacant a number of excellent far-side craters, To one of these, initially assigned to [Rayleigh](/wiki/Rayleigh "Rayleigh"), at 67S, 179E, we have provisionally assigned the name of [Minnaert](/wiki/Minnaert "Minnaert"), to honor the distinguished Dutch astronomer and astrophysicist who had participated so actively in our work on lunar nomenclature prior to his death in October 1970.  
   
 The report includes identifying notes on the names adopted by the IAU in [1964](/wiki/IAU_Transactions_XIIB "IAU Transactions XIIB") (Arthur's list) and in [1961](/wiki/IAU_Transactions_XIB "IAU Transactions XIB") (USSR list), as these data have not been previously available.  
   
 Mr. Robert W. Carder of the [Aeronautical Chart and Information Center](/wiki/DMA "DMA") (of the U.S. Air Force) gave invaluable assistance to the Working Group, providing us first with provisional lunar maps and later with the revised maps and printed overlays, which we used to make the assignments. He also supervised preparations of the Moon maps.  
   
 Grant NGR 22-007-194 from NASA supported a portion of the work of Professor Menzel and the major part of the work of Dr Bell on this project.

**Curie** is a large, degraded [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that lies along western rim and extends into the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_(Moon) "Far side (Moon)") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon").[[3]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-3) Hence, as seen from the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"), it can only be viewed from the side, with visibility depending on the effects of [libration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libration "Libration"). Curie crosses the northern edge of the proposed Australe megabasin. Nearby craters of note include [Schorr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schorr_(crater) "Schorr (crater)") to the northwest and the [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain "Walled plain") called [Sklodowska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sklodowska_(lunar_crater) "Sklodowska (lunar crater)") to the northeast. Attached to the southeastern rim is the heavily damaged walled plain [Lauritsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauritsen_(crater) "Lauritsen (crater)"). Both Sklodowska and Lauritsen are smaller than Curie.[[3]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-3)

This crater is named after French physicist and chemist [Pierre Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Curie "Pierre Curie") (1859–1906).[[4]](#cite_note-Menzel_et_al_1971-4) Its designation was formally adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1970.[[1]](#cite_note-GPN-1)

## Observations

This formation dates to the [Pre-Nectarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Nectarian "Pre-Nectarian") period of the [lunar geologic timescale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_geologic_timescale "Lunar geologic timescale").[[2]](#cite_note-Wilhelms_et_al_1987-2) The outer rim of Curie has been damaged and reshaped by nearby impacts. The sides of the rim are relatively linear, giving the crater an overall box-like shape. The eastern part of the rim is partly overlaid by the notable satellite craters Curie C to the northeast and Curie G along the east. At the northern end the rim is overlaid by the small crater Curie Z. Several other small craters lie along the rim, especially to the southwest.[[5]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-5): 99–100

The interior floor of Curie forms a relatively level plain, at least in comparison to the terrain that surrounds the crater. However this floor is disrupted in several locations by small impacts. A cluster of such impacts lies near the southwestern rim, with several of these craters overlapping each other. The small crater Curie K is located in the southeastern part of the floor, and Curie V lies alongside the northwestern inner wall.[[5]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-5): 99–100

Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Skłodowska-Curie \"Maria Skłodowska-Curie\") |\n\n**Sklodowska** (Skłodowska) is a large [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters \"Lunar craters\") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater \"Impact crater\") that is located on the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_(Moon) \"Far side (Moon)\") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon \"Moon\").[[2]](#cite_note-Moore_2000-2) It lies just past the southeastern limb, and can sometimes be viewed from [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth \"Earth\") under favorable conditions of [libration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libration \"Libration\") and illumination. The crater is located to the northeast of the older [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain \"Walled plain\") named [Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curie_(lunar_crater) \"Curie (lunar crater)\"), and to the southwest of [Pasteur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasteur_(lunar_crater) \"Pasteur (lunar crater)\"), another walled plain.\n\nThis is a prominent crater with a well-defined rim and little appearance of wear from impact erosion. The edge forms a rough circle, but it is irregular with a number of small outward bulges, particularly to the south and southwest. The small crater Sklodowska J intrudes slightly into the southeastern rim.\n\nThe inner walls have a system of multiple terraces, and there are some slumped shelves along the northeastern side. The inner wall is somewhat narrower along the north and wider to the south and northeast. Within the crater the interior floor is a nearly level plain that is marked by a number of small craterlets. There is a prominent central peak formation at the crater midpoint, which consists of two ridges separated by a narrow valley. The larger of the two peaks lies to the northeast of the center, while the smaller is to the southwest. The infrared spectrum of pure crystalline [plagioclase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagioclase \"Plagioclase\") has been identified on this rise.[[3]](#cite_note-Donaldson_Hanna_et_al_2014-3)\n\nThis crater gained its title from the birth name of [Maria Skłodowska-Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie \"Marie Curie\"), the [Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_people \"Polish people\") and [naturalised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalization \"Naturalization\") [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people \"French people\") scientist.\n\n## Views\n\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Sklodowska_(lunar_crater)&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Views\")]\n\n* [![View from Apollo 15](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Sklodowska_crater_AS15-95-12986.jpg/330px-Sklodowska_crater_AS15-95-12986.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sklodowska_crater_AS15-95-12986.jpg \"View from Apollo 15\")\n\n  View from [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 \"Apollo 15\")\n* [![Oblique view from Apollo 15](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Norm

Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Skłodowska-Curie \"Maria Skłodowska-Curie\") |\n\n**Sklodowska** (Skłodowska) is a large [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters \"Lunar craters\") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater \"Impact crater\") that is located on the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_(Moon) \"Far side (Moon)\") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon \"Moon\").[[2]](#cite_note-Moore_2000-2) It lies just past the southeastern limb, and can sometimes be viewed from [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth \"Earth\") under favorable conditions of [libration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libration \"Libration\") and illumination. The crater is located to the northeast of the older [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain \"Walled plain\") named [Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curie_(lunar_crater) \"Curie (lunar crater)\"), and to the southwest of [Pasteur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasteur_(lunar_crater) \"Pasteur (lunar crater)\"), another walled plain.\n\nThis is a prominent crater with a well-defined rim and little appearance of wear from impact erosion. The edge forms a rough circle, but it is irregular with a number of small outward bulges, particularly to the south and southwest. The small crater Sklodowska J intrudes slightly into the southeastern rim.\n\nThe inner walls have a system of multiple terraces, and there are some slumped shelves along the northeastern side. The inner wall is somewhat narrower along the north and wider to the south and northeast. Within the crater the interior floor is a nearly level plain that is marked by a number of small craterlets. There is a prominent central peak formation at the crater midpoint, which consists of two ridges separated by a narrow valley. The larger of the two peaks lies to the northeast of the center, while the smaller is to the southwest. The infrared spectrum of pure crystalline [plagioclase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagioclase \"Plagioclase\") has been identified on this rise.[[3]](#cite_note-Donaldson_Hanna_et_al_2014-3)\n\nThis crater gained its title from the birth name of [Maria Skłodowska-Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie \"Marie Curie\"), the [Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_people \"Polish people\") and [naturalised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalization \"Naturalization\") [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people \"French people\") scientist.\n\n## Views\n\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Sklodowska_(lunar_crater)&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Views\")]\n\n* [![View from Apollo 15](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Sklodowska_crater_AS15-95-12986.jpg/330px-Sklodowska_crater_AS15-95-12986.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sklodowska_crater_AS15-95-12986.jpg \"View from Apollo 15\")\n\n  View from [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 \"Apollo 15\")\n* [![Oblique view from Apollo 15](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Norm

Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Skłodowska-Curie \"Maria Skłodowska-Curie\") |\n\n**Sklodowska** (Skłodowska) is a large [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters \"Lunar craters\") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater \"Impact crater\") that is located on the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_(Moon) \"Far side (Moon)\") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon \"Moon\").[[2]](#cite_note-Moore_2000-2) It lies just past the southeastern limb, and can sometimes be viewed from [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth \"Earth\") under favorable conditions of [libration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libration \"Libration\") and illumination. The crater is located to the northeast of the older [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain \"Walled plain\") named [Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curie_(lunar_crater) \"Curie (lunar crater)\"), and to the southwest of [Pasteur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasteur_(lunar_crater) \"Pasteur (lunar crater)\"), another walled plain.\n\nThis is a prominent crater with a well-defined rim and little appearance of wear from impact erosion. The edge forms a rough circle, but it is irregular with a number of small outward bulges, particularly to the south and southwest. The small crater Sklodowska J intrudes slightly into the southeastern rim.\n\nThe inner walls have a system of multiple terraces, and there are some slumped shelves along the northeastern side. The inner wall is somewhat narrower along the north and wider to the south and northeast. Within the crater the interior floor is a nearly level plain that is marked by a number of small craterlets. There is a prominent central peak formation at the crater midpoint, which consists of two ridges separated by a narrow valley. The larger of the two peaks lies to the northeast of the center, while the smaller is to the southwest. The infrared spectrum of pure crystalline [plagioclase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagioclase \"Plagioclase\") has been identified on this rise.[[3]](#cite_note-Donaldson_Hanna_et_al_2014-3)\n\nThis crater gained its title from the birth name of [Maria Skłodowska-Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie \"Marie Curie\"), the [Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_people \"Polish people\") and [naturalised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalization \"Naturalization\") [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people \"French people\") scientist.\n\n## Views\n\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Sklodowska_(lunar_crater)&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Views\")]\n\n* [![View from Apollo 15](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Sklodowska_crater_AS15-95-12986.jpg/330px-Sklodowska_crater_AS15-95-12986.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sklodowska_crater_AS15-95-12986.jpg \"View from Apollo 15\")\n\n  View from [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 \"Apollo 15\")\n* [![Oblique view from Apollo 15](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Norm

Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Skłodowska-Curie \"Maria Skłodowska-Curie\") |\n\n**Sklodowska** (Skłodowska) is a large [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters \"Lunar craters\") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater \"Impact crater\") that is located on the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_(Moon) \"Far side (Moon)\") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon \"Moon\").[[2]](#cite_note-Moore_2000-2) It lies just past the southeastern limb, and can sometimes be viewed from [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth \"Earth\") under favorable conditions of [libration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libration \"Libration\") and illumination. The crater is located to the northeast of the older [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain \"Walled plain\") named [Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curie_(lunar_crater) \"Curie (lunar crater)\"), and to the southwest of [Pasteur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasteur_(lunar_crater) \"Pasteur (lunar crater)\"), another walled plain.\n\nThis is a prominent crater with a well-defined rim and little appearance of wear from impact erosion. The edge forms a rough circle, but it is irregular with a number of small outward bulges, particularly to the south and southwest. The small crater Sklodowska J intrudes slightly into the southeastern rim.\n\nThe inner walls have a system of multiple terraces, and there are some slumped shelves along the northeastern side. The inner wall is somewhat narrower along the north and wider to the south and northeast. Within the crater the interior floor is a nearly level plain that is marked by a number of small craterlets. There is a prominent central peak formation at the crater midpoint, which consists of two ridges separated by a narrow valley. The larger of the two peaks lies to the northeast of the center, while the smaller is to the southwest. The infrared spectrum of pure crystalline [plagioclase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagioclase \"Plagioclase\") has been identified on this rise.[[3]](#cite_note-Donaldson_Hanna_et_al_2014-3)\n\nThis crater gained its title from the birth name of [Maria Skłodowska-Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie \"Marie Curie\"), the [Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_people \"Polish people\") and [naturalised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalization \"Naturalization\") [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people \"French people\") scientist.\n\n## Views\n\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Sklodowska_(lunar_crater)&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Views\")]\n\n* [![View from Apollo 15](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Sklodowska_crater_AS15-95-12986.jpg/330px-Sklodowska_crater_AS15-95-12986.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sklodowska_crater_AS15-95-12986.jpg \"View from Apollo 15\")\n\n  View from [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 \"Apollo 15\")\n* [![Oblique view from Apollo 15](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Norm

Oblique view of Thomson from [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15")

**Thomson** is a [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that is located within the [Mare Ingenii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mare_Ingenii "Mare Ingenii") on the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_of_the_Moon "Far side of the Moon") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon").[[1]](#cite_note-Moore_2000-1) Just to the northeast is the unusual merged crater formation of [Van de Graaff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_de_Graaff_(crater) "Van de Graaff (crater)"). On the northwest rim of the [mare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_mare "Lunar mare") is [O'Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O'Day_(crater) "O'Day (crater)"), and to the south-southwest is [Obruchev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obruchev_(crater) "Obruchev (crater)") on the southern shore of Mare Ingenii.

In the past the crater was flooded by [lava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lava "Lava"), leaving only the outer rim intact. There are gaps in the eastern and western rims, leaving two "half-moon" mountainous formations facing each other across the relatively flat floor. There is a similar lava-flooded crater remnant attached to the southern rim of Thomson. The floor of Thomson has a number of secondary impacts that form short, linear streaks across the surface. The infrared spectrum of pure crystalline [plagioclase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagioclase "Plagioclase") has been identified on the northwest rim.[[2]](#cite_note-Donaldson_Hanna_et_al_2014-2)

**Hess** is a degraded [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_craters "Lunar craters") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that lies in the southern hemisphere on the [far side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_of_the_Moon "Far side of the Moon").[[1]](#cite_note-Moore_2000-1) On the [lunar geologic timescale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_geologic_timescale "Lunar geologic timescale"), Hess dates from the [Pre-Nectarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Nectarian "Pre-Nectarian") period.[[2]](#cite_note-Purohit_et_al_2018-2) The crater rim has been worn by subsequent impacts, leaving a low, eroded outer wall. The flat interior has been resurfaced by [lava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lava "Lava") flows and is free of significant impacts. This floor has a slightly darker [albedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albedo "Albedo") than the surrounding terrain.

The crater [Boyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyle_(crater) "Boyle (crater)") is nearly attached to the northeastern rim of Hess, and [Abbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbe_(crater) "Abbe (crater)") lies to the south. To the west is a large [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain "Walled plain") named [Poincaré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincaré_(crater) "Poincaré (crater)"), and Hess is located at the eastern edge of the crater's deeply eroded outer rim. The satellite crater Hess Z is partly overlaid by the northern rim of Hess. The small crater Hess M joins the south-southwest rim of Hess to the northwest rim of Abbe.

**Michelson** is a [crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_(Moon) "Far side (Moon)") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon").[[1]](#cite_note-Moore_2000-1) It lies along the northeastern outer rim of a huge [walled plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walled_plain "Walled plain") called [Hertzsprung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertzsprung_(crater) "Hertzsprung (crater)"), and to the southwest of the crater [Kolhörster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolhörster_(crater) "Kolhörster (crater)").

This is a heavily eroded crater formation with multiple impacts along the rim edge and within the interior. The rim is roughly circular, but has been rendered relatively uneven due to these smaller craters. There are small craters across the interior floor, including impacts along the northern, western and southeastern edges. The infrared spectrum of pure crystalline [plagioclase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagioclase "Plagioclase") has been identified on the southwest floor.[[2]](#cite_note-Donaldson_Hanna_et_al_2014-2)

To the southeast of the outer rim is a crater chain that has been designated Catena Michelson. This feature is radial to the [Mare Orientale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mare_Orientale "Mare Orientale") impact basin, and passes near the outer rim of the crater [Grachev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grachev_(crater) "Grachev (crater)").
